strengths: Comprehensive and methodologically careful empirical study: the paper systematically ablates key design choices (report length augmentation, patch size/FOV, token aggregation, batch size/loss type, augmentation strength) for 3D CLIP-style pre-training, which the community genuinely lacks and which yields transferable best practices beyond the specific model.

First work to combine vision–language objectives (contrastive + radiology report generation à la CapPa) with a vision-only objective (MAE) in the 3D medical imaging domain, and to leverage both paired (CT-RATE) and unpaired (NLST) data in a single VLE training recipe.

Holistic evaluation across four task families (retrieval, linear probing, zero-shot classification, report generation, segmentation) with an honest, nuanced discussion: the authors do not hide that added objectives reduce probing/zero-shot performance, that MAE beats their encoders on segmentation, and that prompt formulation strongly affects zero-shot results.

Report generation evaluation is notably more rigorous than prior 3D work: beyond lexical metrics, clinical fidelity metrics (RadBERT classifier, RadFact-CT (+/-) and (+) variants) are introduced and show large, meaningful gains (+17 MacroF1, +7 RadFact (+)) over baselines, with an insightful analysis of the (+/-) metric masking low diagnostic sensitivity.

Good experimental hygiene: pre-training data is split off from downstream evaluation to prevent leakage, probe selection is done on a held-out validation set and transferred as-is to test, extensive appendix details (preprocessing, prompts, metrics, training recipes) support reproducibility.

Honest and substantive limitations section that correctly identifies prompt brittleness and the mismatch between voxel-level MIM and embedding-level contrastive objectives, and proposes informed future directions (e.g., iBOT-style objectives).
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: the method is essentially SigLIP 2-style combination of CLIP + captioning + MAE transplanted to 3D medical imaging with domain-specific tweaks (GPT-4o report shortening/structuring, sentence shuffling). For readers familiar with [24, 26, 42, 43], the core recipe is a well-executed adaptation rather than a new idea.

Headline claims are somewhat overstated relative to the evidence: the abstract claims state-of-the-art in zero-shot classification, but on CT-RATE COLIPRI-C (77.8 AUROC) only ties fVLM and falls behind on RAD-ChestCT; 'competitive' would be more accurate. The strongest genuine SOTA claims are classification probing and report generation clinical metrics.

Dense-task story is weak: segmentation results show MAE pre-training dominating all COLIPRI variants, and the combined MAE objective provides no segmentation benefit (COLIPRI-CM/CRM often worse than COLIPRI-C), suggesting the third contribution does not yet deliver its intended value for its primary motivation.

Ablation tables appear to be single runs without confidence intervals, while many reported deltas between configurations are small (e.g., 0.1–0.5 AUROC), making several hyperparameter conclusions potentially noise-driven; only the report generation results include bootstrap intervals.

Baseline comparisons have caveats the authors themselves acknowledge: the re-evaluated CT-CLIP performs anomalously poorly ('potential configuration issue'), forcing reliance on third-party reported numbers with different abnormality subsets (fVLM excludes 2 of 18 classes), so zero-shot comparisons are not fully apples-to-apples.

Heavy dependence on GPT-4o for report re-translation, structuring, and shortening introduces potential leakage of external knowledge into training text and complicates reproducibility/cost; the native-vs-short prompting scheme also effectively requires report-derived class embeddings for evaluation, limiting practical zero-shot utility.
Scope restricted to chest CT; generalisation of the 'best practices' to other organs/modalities (despite the framing of 'comprehensive 3D medical image understanding') is untested.

strengths: The paper tackles a genuinely important and under-explored problem: scaling vision-language pre-training to 3D medical imaging under severe data constraints, and positions itself well against prior 3D VLEs (CT-CLIP, Merlin, fVLM).

The experimental program is unusually thorough for the field: dozens of full pre-training runs ablating text augmentation, FOV/patch size, token aggregation, batch size, RRG objective (depth, loss weight, causal vs. parallel captioning), and MAE integration (masking ratio/style, decoder depth, late inclusion). This constitutes a useful 'best practices' reference for 3D medical VLE training.

The domain-specific observations are insightful and well-motivated, particularly the report-length distribution shift motivating Sentence Shuffle / Sentence Shortening augmentations, and the analysis of long structured reports vs. short zero-shot prompts.

The report generation results are convincing: large clinical-metric gains (+17 RadBERT MacroF1, +7 RadFact-CT/F1 (+)) over established baselines, with a sensible discussion of why lexical metrics are misleading and why (+/-) metrics can mask low diagnostic sensitivity.

The limitations section is honest and substantive: the authors openly report that segmentation lags a plain MAE baseline, that the added objectives hurt linear probing and native zero-shot classification, and that prompt sensitivity is a real weakness, rather than overselling the method.
Evaluation spans multiple task families (retrieval, probing, zero-shot, report generation, segmentation) on two datasets, with attention to pre-training/downstream leakage via re-splitting CT-RATE.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited: COLIPRI is essentially SigLIP 2-style combination of CLIP + generative captioning (CapPa) + MAE transferred to 3D CT, with domain-tuned augmentations. As an Algorithms/General contribution (the natural reading, despite the systems-flavored framing), the conceptual advance over [42, 43, 24, 26] applied to a new domain is incremental.

The headline 'state-of-the-art' claim does not hold uniformly. Zero-shot classification trails fVLM on both CT-RATE and RAD-ChestCT, and segmentation falls clearly behind a simple MAE pre-trained encoder on all three datasets; only classification probing and report generation show clear wins. The abstract's claim of SOTA in 'report generation, classification probing, and zero-shot classification' overstates the third item.

The 'native' zero-shot prompting scheme, under which COLIPRI performs best, constructs class prototypes from 50 real patient reports per abnormality. This is a favorable, test-distribution-matched protocol that cannot be applied to the published baseline numbers (taken from fVLM), making the zero-shot comparison asymmetric and potentially inflating COLIPRI's standing relative to baselines evaluated with simple prompts.

Heavy reliance on GPT-4o for core pipeline components raises reproducibility and circularity concerns: report re-translation, structuring, and shortening all use GPT-4o, and the primary clinical evaluation metric (RadFact-CT) is also GPT-4o-based. The paper does not release the GPT-4o-processed corpus, and the resulting model is partially conditioned on a proprietary, non-reproducible preprocessing step.

The manuscript does not clearly commit to releasing code, pre-trained weights, or the processed reports. For a paper whose main value is 'best practices for 3D medical VLE training', reproducibility is essential, and its absence substantially reduces the practical impact.

Absolute performance is weak across the board (retrieval R@1 ~16%, zero-shot AUROC ~75-78%, clinical report F1 ~20-40%), and the paper does not provide statistical significance testing for the headline comparisons, despite reporting confidence intervals only in Tab. 9. Given the many ablation decisions made on a single validation split with small validation sets, some 'optimal' choices may not be robust.

Several findings are acknowledged but unexplained, weakening the scientific case for the proposed objective combination: adding the RRG objective (explicitly designed to help) reduces probing and zero-shot performance; adding MAE barely helps or hurts segmentation. This suggests the composite recipe is not yet well understood, and the ablation-driven design risks overfitting to the CT-RATE validation split.

The development protocol trains and selects on one modality/region (chest CT) with a single architecture (Primus-M) and a single text encoder choice justified by limited ablation; generalization of the 'best practices' beyond this narrow setting is asserted rather than demonstrated.

strengths: Comprehensive and well-motivated empirical study: the paper systematically ablates CLIP training design choices (report length/augmentation, patch size, FOV, token aggregation, batch size, loss type, augmentation strength) in the 3D medical domain, which is valuable given how under-explored this setting is and how different it is from 2D natural images.

The proposed COLIPRI family (CLIP + CapPa-style report generation + MAE) sensibly transfers recent ideas from natural-image pre-training (SigLIP 2 / CapPa / LocCa) to 3D medical imaging, with domain-specific innovations such as sentence shuffling, LLM-based sentence shortening, and structured report generation that addresses the long-report/short-prompt distribution shift — a genuinely interesting and well-analysed problem specific to radiology.

Strong empirical results across a wide evaluation suite: SOTA on classification probing, competitive-to-SOTA zero-shot classification, and substantially improved clinical fidelity of report generation (+17 RadBERT MacroF1, +7 RadFact-CT F1(+)) versus strong baselines (CT-CLIP, CT-FM, Merlin, fVLM), on two datasets (CT-RATE, RAD-ChestCT).

Honest, transparent reporting: the paper openly reports where added objectives (RRG, MAE) reduce global-task performance, shows segmentation results lag behind MAE pre-training, discusses limitations (prompt sensitivity, dense-task mismatch) in a dedicated section, and even flags potential configuration issues when comparing against released baseline checkpoints.

Good reproducibility posture: extensive appendix with data preprocessing, prompts, metrics, probe training details, and full result tables; uses public datasets (CT-RATE, NLST, RAD-ChestCT) with explicit handling of pre-training/downstream data leakage.

Appropriately declared contribution type (Algorithms/General with strong Applied components): the methodological novelties are incremental but the systematic 'best practices for 3D medical VLEs' study and the open encoder family constitute a meaningful contribution to the community.
weaknesses: Zero-shot results rely heavily on the 'native' prompting scheme, which averages embeddings of 50 real CT-RATE reports per abnormality. This raises concerns about circularity: prompts are drawn from the same distribution (and possibly the same dataset) as the training data, making the headline zero-shot comparison against baselines evaluated only with short prompts (values taken from fVLM) potentially unfair. The authors acknowledge this asymmetry but do not fully resolve it; baselines could not be re-evaluated with native prompting.

The final model COLIPRI-CRM is not the best model on any single global metric: COLIPRI-C is best for probing, COLIPRI-CR for retrieval. The added RRG and MAE objectives reduce classification probing and native zero-shot performance relative to COLIPRI-C, so the practical value of the 'comprehensive' combination is partially undercut — although report generation results favour the composite models.

Segmentation fine-tuning results show only marginal gains over training from scratch (and are clearly worse than pure MAE pre-training), meaning the proposed pre-training has limited benefit for dense tasks despite this being a stated motivation for the MAE component.

No direct retrieval comparison against external baselines in the final experiments (retrieval appears only in internal ablations), and statistical significance of several differences is not established (the authors themselves note some gaps are within confidence intervals).

Dependence on GPT-4o for report translation, structuring, and shortening introduces cost, non-determinism, and potential biases that are not deeply analysed; the RadFact-CT evaluation also relies on GPT-4o as a judge.

Several presentation issues remain (e.g., 'Out comprehensive' in Fig. 1 caption, 'an large language model', a duplicated positive-finding definition in A.2, minor table inconsistencies such as COLIPRI-CM's zero-shot(S) being selected on validation yet degrading on final evaluation), suggesting the manuscript would benefit from another careful editing pass.
Scope is limited to chest CT; claims of 'comprehensive' 3D medical understanding would be strengthened by at least one additional organ/modality, though the datasets used justify the current scope.

strengths: Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation spanning zero-shot classification, linear probing, retrieval, report generation, and segmentation fine-tuning, with appropriate statistical treatment (bootstrap CIs) and multi-task assessment of the encoder family.

The Opposite Sentence Loss (OSL) is a genuinely novel and well-motivated contribution addressing the training–inference distribution shift between long radiology reports and short diagnostic queries; Table 3 convincingly demonstrates it closes a large zero-shot gap (~7 AUROC points).

The combination of vision–language and vision-only (MAE) objectives is shown to be complementary: global tasks benefit from multimodal alignment while dense tasks benefit from MAE, and Tab. D.5 carefully isolates the effect of MAE initialisation.

Extensive, transparent ablation studies (Tables B.1–B.10) covering text augmentations, FOV, patch size, pooling, loss types, masking strategies, and hyperparameters — this is unusually thorough and supports reproducibility.

Clinically meaningful evaluation of report generation (RadBERT F1, RadFact-CT variants) rather than relying solely on lexical overlap, and a thoughtful discussion of the positive/negative findings imbalance; honest limitations section acknowledging the low absolute clinical performance.
Model weights, code, and usage examples are promised to be released; preprocessing details (including GPT-4o prompts in Sec. E) are fully disclosed, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The contribution is largely an engineering synthesis of established techniques (CLIP, CapPa-style captioning, MAE) adapted to 3D medical imaging; the conceptual novelty is limited to OSL and the domain adaptation choices, which may reduce impact for the broader vision community.

Some reported gains may partly stem from advantages not attributable to the method itself: the authors state their multi-probe setup (multiple pooling schemes and learning rates selected on validation) yields substantially higher baselines than prior work, making comparisons to published numbers not fully apples-to-apples; zero-shot baseline numbers for fVLM, Merlin, etc. are taken from [37] rather than recomputed under the same short-prompt protocol.

The RRG objective, advertised as a main contribution (contribution 2), yields only marginal improvements and the authors themselves concede it has minimal impact on report generation and slight negative effects on classification; its justification is weakened by the authors' own analysis.

Zero-shot classification still lags substantially behind supervised probes (~86 vs ~80 AUROC), and segmentation performance remains below CNN references (ResEnc-L) on most datasets, limiting the claim of a general-purpose foundation encoder.

Evaluation is confined to chest CT (CT-RATE, NLST) and chest/upper-abdomen segmentation tasks; generalisation to other anatomical regions, modalities, and truly external datasets (beyond RAD-ChestCT, which is derived from similar distributions) is not demonstrated.

Dependence on GPT-4o for report restructuring, shortening, and labeling introduces potential for processing errors and questions about the scalability and consistency of the pipeline; no analysis of LLM preprocessing error rates is provided.

Minor issues: some typos ('Why hypothesise', 'createantialiasing', 'classfication'), Table 2 excludes two abnormalities 'to be consistent with [37]' which complicates direct comparison, and the Mermaid-style model naming (C/CR/CM/CRM) takes effort to track.

strengths: Comprehensive and well-organised empirical study: the paper systematically stages its model (COLIPRI-C/CR/CM/CRM) and evaluates across zero-shot classification, linear probes, retrieval, report generation, and 5-fold cross-validated semantic segmentation on four public datasets, with confidence intervals and extended results in the appendix.

The ablation material (Tabs. B.1-B.10) is unusually thorough for this domain, covering report augmentations, text encoder choice, field of view, patch size, token aggregation, batch size/loss type, RRG and MAE hyperparameters, and MAE initialisation (Tab. D.5), giving the community genuine guidance on adapting CLIP-style pre-training to 3D CT.

The Opposite Sentence Loss (OSL) is a sensible, clearly motivated idea (Sec. B.4, Algorithm 1) that directly addresses the train/inference text-length distribution shift, and Tab. 3 quantifies its effect on short-prompt zero-shot classification (~+7.5 AUROC).

Strong reported results: the COLIPRI-CM/CRM encoders exceed prior 3D VLE baselines on classification probes, zero-shot classification, retrieval (R@5 35.1% vs 2.9% for CT-CLIP), and clinical report-generation metrics, and match or beat MAE pre-training on segmentation; PCA visualisations qualitatively support better dense features.

Honest treatment of limitations: the authors acknowledge the modest impact of the RRG objective, the large probe-vs-zero-shot gap, the remaining gap to ResEnc-L on dense tasks, and that clinical metrics are below practice thresholds. Model weights, code, and prompts (GPT-4o translation/structuring/shortening) are promised for release, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is arguably incremental: the framework largely assembles known components (CLIP contrastive loss, CapPa-style captioning, MAE from nnSSL, Primus-M/CXR-BERT backbones). The claim that 'no work has combined self-supervised and vision-language objectives' appears overreaching. The core contribution is closer to careful engineering/systems work than a new algorithmic idea, which should be stated and assessed as such.

Heavy, unvalidated dependence on GPT-4o for the critical report preprocessing pipeline (translation, structuring into 8 subsections, positive/negative finding extraction, shortening). No quantitative evaluation of this preprocessing is provided (e.g., accuracy of LLM-assigned labels), yet the OSL supervision labels and short-prompt training all inherit potential LLM errors. This is a significant soundness concern for the headline zero-shot claims.

Potential circularity in evaluation: GPT-4o is used both to create the training data style (shortened, structured findings) and as the judge in RadFact-CT, one of the main clinical report-generation metrics. The large RadFact/RadBERT gains may partly reflect stylistic alignment with the LLM-generated text distribution rather than genuinely better clinical understanding; an independent evaluation would strengthen the claim.

Evaluation is largely confined to chest CT and, for the main VLE tasks, to CT-RATE-derived test sets plus RAD-ChestCT (which itself uses CT-RATE-derived abnormality classes). Retrieval and zero-shot results are reported only on CT-RATE; no external, out-of-distribution clinical cohort or multi-organ evaluation for the vision-language tasks is provided, limiting support for the 'general-purpose 3D medical encoder' framing.

Some ablation and main results are mixed and weaken the narrative: COLIPRI-C and COLIPRI-CR underperform simple baselines on several tasks (e.g., zero-shot on RAD-ChestCT, retrieval vs. no-RRG variants), and the authors themselves show the RRG objective adds little to report generation; the final COLIPRI-CRM merges optimised configurations 'without further ablations', so the interaction of all four objectives is not verified.

The 'linear probing' protocol is not strictly linear: five aggregation schemes including learned attention-pooling heads are swept with four learning rates and the best selected on validation (Sec. C.2), which advantages flexible probes and complicates the claim that the paper's probe numbers are 'more suited for comparison'. Absolute probe values (AUROC ~86%) also cannot be directly compared to baselines evaluated under the original protocol, as the authors concede for CT-CLIP.

Absolute clinical quality remains low (RadBERT MacroF1 ~45%, RadFact-CT(+) F1 ~22%), and the paper does not include any clinician-based evaluation or safety/error analysis, which limits the practical significance of the RRG improvements despite the large relative gains over weak baselines.

strengths: This is a thorough and well-executed empirical/systems contribution to 3D medical vision–language pre-training. The staged COLIPRI-C → CR → CM → CRM development allows the reader to attribute gains to each objective (CLIP, OSL, RRG, MAE), and the appendix ablations (Tabs. B.1–B.10) are unusually extensive and carefully designed (report augmentations, FOV/patch size, token aggregation, loss type, MAE masking, etc.).

The Opposite Sentence Loss (OSL) is a genuinely novel and well-motivated contribution: it directly addresses a real, quantified train–inference mismatch (long reports at training vs. short negated prompts at inference), and Tab. 3/B.1 demonstrates it closes a ~10-point AUROC gap in short-form zero-shot classification without requiring spatial grounding as in fVLM or Merlin.

Combining a vision-only MAE objective with the vision–language objectives is well argued and validated: it enables leveraging the large image-only NLST corpus, yields the largest gains in classification/retrieval, and the MAE-initialisation ablation (Tab. D.5) cleanly shows its importance for dense tasks.

Evaluation breadth is a major strength: classification probes, zero-shot classification, report generation (with clinical metrics RadBERT and a CT-adapted RadFact, including the insightful (+) vs. (+/–) analysis on negative findings), retrieval, and semantic segmentation fine-tuning on four datasets with five-fold CV and confidence intervals.

The authors are commendably transparent: they report both their own computed baseline numbers and literature values where a configuration discrepancy exists (CT-CLIP), discuss that RRG adds little downstream benefit, note the remaining probe-vs-zero-shot gap, and honestly state that performance remains below clinical thresholds. Models, code, and prompts (appendix E) are released, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is moderate: the framework is largely a careful assembly of existing components (CLIP, CapPa-style captioning, MAE, Primus-M, CXR-BERT) adapted to 3D. The main algorithmic novelty is the OSL; most other design decisions are domain adaptations validated by ablation. This is acceptable for the contribution type, but the paper's framing as a comprehensive pre-training recipe rather than a new method should be kept in mind when judging significance.

All pre-training and most evaluation are chest-CT specific (CT-RATE, NLST, RAD-ChestCT). The claimed SOTA/encoder-family generality is untested on other anatomies, modalities, or non-contrast settings; segmentation datasets partially cover upper abdomen, but the encoder's transfer beyond chest CT remains an open question.

Some baseline comparisons are weakened by heterogeneous evaluation setups: zero-shot values for CT-CLIP, BIUD, Merlin, and fVLM are taken from Shui et al. rather than reproduced, and the authors' own probing setup yields systematically higher numbers for all methods (e.g., CT-CLIP performing far below its reported values), making cross-paper comparisons less reliable even with the disclosed caveats.

The RRG objective, one of the three claimed contributions, shows minimal downstream benefit for report generation (Sec. 5.3) and mixed effects on classification; the authors acknowledge this, but it weakens the completeness of the 'comprehensive' recipe narrative.

Dependence on GPT-4o for report translation, structuring, and shortening introduces a proprietary, partially non-reproducible preprocessing pipeline, and the RadFact-CT evaluation relies on GPT-4o with adapted prompts; the sensitivity of results to these LLM choices is not analysed.

Transformer-based encoders still trail CNN references (ResEnc-L) on segmentation, and absolute clinical accuracy of generated reports remains low (RadFact-CT (+) F1 ~22%), so practical clinical impact, despite SOTA claims, is still distant — appropriately acknowledged in the limitations.
